title: John of the Cross in prison
hookLine: imprisoned by his own brothers, he writes poems of love in a tiny cell, then escapes

lines: LOCKED UP BY HIS OWN BROTHERS.
cards: The cell is tiny, tradition says, little more than a closet, with light only from a narrow opening high in the wall. The man inside is a small, quiet friar who has been helping Teresa's reform among the men of her order.
One night, friars of his own order who opposed the reform came and took him. Now they keep him locked in this cell in Toledo. He is brought out to be scolded, and, accounts say, beaten.
Little light, almost nothing to read, the same clothes day after day. And in the dark he starts composing love poems in his head, memorizing them, since there's nothing to write with.

teach.h: OUT A HIGH WINDOW, BY NIGHT.
teach.b: Later, the story goes, a kinder jailer gave him a little paper and ink, and he wrote some of the poems down. Then one night he got out through a high window and slipped away to a convent of Teresa's nuns, who hid him.
Much of what he wrote is love poetry. Some hear an echo of the Song of Songs, where the beloved goes searching at night.
In the King James Bible: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth."

One of his poems begins, in Spanish, en una noche oscura: on a dark night. A soul slips out of a quiet house, unseen, with no light to guide it except the one burning in the heart, and goes to meet the beloved.
Scholars debate which poems were made in that cell. But the shape of the prison is in them: darkness, escape, a night that turns out to be the way to love.

Later he wrote long explanations of the poem, and from them comes the idea behind a phrase people still use: the dark night of the soul. In ordinary speech it means a terrible stretch. For John it's more.
It's a time when the usual lights go out, prayer feels empty, and God, he says, is working in the dark where we can't see.

teach.h: DARKNESS AND LIGHT, ALIKE TO GOD.
teach.b: A psalm says: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." The friar in the closet wrote love songs with almost no light.

how: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; Carmelites and others read his poems and his writing on the dark night, and Christians of different churches turn to them in seasons when prayer feels empty.

games.q: John of the Cross in prison — tap the pairs.

s: John was imprisoned by enemies of the church
friars of his own order, who opposed Teresa's reform, locked him up.
for John, the dark night just means a bad stretch
he describes a time when the usual lights go out and God works where we can't see.
he composed poems in his head before he could write them down
with nothing to write with, he memorized them. later, the story goes, a kinder jailer gave him a little paper and ink.

games.q: you're John, locked in a tiny cell with little light and nothing to write with. what do you do with the dark?
o: compose love poems in your head and memorize them.
write angry letters to your jailers.
games.why: he composes poems and keeps them in memory. later, with a little paper and ink, he writes some down.

practice: Let something hard come to mind, in your life or the world, without fixing it.
Then look gently for one beautiful thing beside it, a kindness, a face, a small mercy, and shape it into one line of a poem, kept in your head the way John did.
If you pray, offer the line to God; if you don't, let it sit beside the hard thing.

wordCard.voice: Noche oscura. Spanish for dark night, the opening phrase of John of the Cross's poem, about a soul slipping out to meet its love.

orig.note: Spanish (Latin alphabet, the original language of the poem): dark night, from the opening of John's poem, en una noche oscura.
